books.section: The Election of 1896 and the “Cross of Gold” Speech
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text: In 1896, William Jennings Bryan won the Democratic presidential nomination with his “Cross of Gold” speech calling for the free coinage of silver, and the People’s Party also nominated him. The Republican William McKinley, who stood for the gold standard, campaigned from his front porch in Canton, Ohio, receiving visitors instead of traveling. His campaign manager, Mark Hanna, raised far more money than Bryan’s campaign spent. McKinley won with 51 percent of the popular vote, and Republicans went on to dominate national politics for a generation. Every winner from 1876 through 1892 had taken less than half the popular vote. The last majority before 1896 was Grant’s in 1872.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts, grounded in Barron’s Chapter 8, Topic 6.13, and 5 Steps Chapter 18.

stem: Why did the People's Party also nominate Bryan in 1896?

options.text: Bryan promised to end all government regulation of the railroads
options.misconception: Populists wanted more railroad regulation, and Bryan agreed with them.

options.text: Bryan backed free silver, the Populists' central demand
Bryan was a Republican who had left McKinley's party
options.misconception: Bryan was the Democratic nominee, not a Republican defector.

options.text: Bryan promised to keep the country on the gold standard
options.misconception: Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech attacked the gold standard.

rationales.A: Populists wanted more railroad regulation, and Bryan agreed with them.
rationales.B: Free silver at 16 to 1 was the demand Bryan and the Populists shared.
rationales.C: Bryan led the Democrats, and the Populists joined him.
rationales.D: Bryan's famous speech denounced crucifixion on a cross of gold.
rationales.general:
Find the demand Bryan and the Populists shared.
1. Bryan won his nomination with the 'Cross of Gold' speech for free silver.
2. Free silver at 16 to 1 was the Populists' central demand.
3. The People's Party backed the candidate who carried its cause.
4. Sharing one great demand can fuse two parties behind one man.
Remember: parties join forces where their programs overlap.
